title: What makes us yawn?
summary: Josh and Chuck explore why people yawn, covering the involuntary nature of yawning, fetal yawning in utero, the stretch-yawn called pendiculation, and contagious yawning. They review theories including oxygen deprivation and carbon dioxide (ruled out by Robert Provine's experiments), boredom, Hippocrates' fever idea, alertness/arousal, evolutionary signaling, and the brain-cooling theory (currently favored, with outside temperature studies by Gallup and colleagues). They discuss research linking contagious yawning to empathy and autism, which they find questionable. The episode closes with a listener mail about Rodriguez, the singer-songwriter from Searching for Sugar Man, and a recommendation of documentaries.

segments.title: Opening banter and pendiculating
segments.summary: Hosts open with banter about Florida smear campaigns using technical terms, then discuss pendiculating (yawn-stretch) and how yawning is contagious.

segments.title: Yawning as involuntary; fetal yawning
segments.summary: Yawning is described as involuntary. Fetuses have been observed yawning from eleven to twenty weeks, which undercuts the oxygenation theory. A paralysis case shows a paralyzed arm can still rise during a deep yawn.

segments.title: Physiology of a yawn
segments.summary: Describes the physical sequence of a yawn: mouth opens, eyes close, lungs fill and exhale, and neurotransmitters such as dopamine are activated. Robert Provine views yawns as marking a shift between arousal states; surfactant distribution in the lungs is mentioned as a process but not a confirmed purpose.

segments.title: Yawning theories: boredom and oxygen/carbon dioxide
segments.summary: The boredom theory is dismissed. The oxygen and carbon dioxide theory is tested by Provine, who gave athletes extra oxygen and raised ambient carbon dioxide; yawning continued, so the theory is ruled out.

segments.title: Evolutionary and brain-cooling theories
segments.summary: Evolutionary ideas include baring teeth to intimidate and a signal for hunters to coordinate. The brain-cooling theory is described as the most recent and currently favored explanation.

segments.title: Empathy, autism and contagious yawning
segments.summary: Contagious yawning is linked to empathy. Studies found people with autism, especially at stronger points on the spectrum, yawn less contagiously, though the hosts question these studies, noting autistic children focus on mouths rather than eyes. Hippocrates' early fever idea and the 17th-18th century alertness view are mentioned.

segments.title: Heart rate, outside temperature and research uncertainty
segments.summary: Yawning briefly raises heart rate during inhalation. Gallup and colleagues found warmer outside temperatures reduce yawning, consistent with brain cooling, while other tests showed yawning rises with brain temperature. The hosts note how much remains unknown.

segments.title: Yawn and orgasm connection and closing thoughts
segments.summary: Provine says yawns and orgasms may share a neuro-behavioral heritage. The hosts conclude yawning remains a mystery and joke about watching pets and Emily's stretching.

segments.title: Listener mail: Rodriguez in Detroit
segments.summary: Listener Julia recounts meeting Rodriguez at a Detroit bar and hearing him play a new song three times on a picnic table in her courtyard. She mentions the film Searching for Sugar Man, and the hosts recommend documentaries How to Survive a Plague and No Place on Earth.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts invite listeners to search the topic on the website and send in stories and email, then sign off.
